q: What is the Taj Mahal?
alts: tell me about the taj mahal
a:
The Taj Mahal is an ivory-white marble **mausoleum** on the south bank of the Yamuna river in **Agra, India**. The Mughal emperor **Shah Jahan** commissioned it in 1631 as a tomb for his favourite wife, **Mumtaz Mahal**, and he was later buried there beside her.

The tomb is the centrepiece of a 17-hectare complex with a mosque, a guest house (the jawab), a great gate and a formal charbagh garden. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the New 7 Wonders of the World.

q: Who built the Taj Mahal?
a:
It was commissioned by **Shah Jahan**, the fifth Mughal emperor (ruled 1628–1658), in memory of his wife **Mumtaz Mahal**.

The actual work was led by a board of architects under **Ustad Ahmad Lahori**, the emperor's court architect, and carried out by more than **20,000** workers and artisans.

q: Why was the Taj Mahal built?
alts: what was the reason for building it
why did shah jahan build it
what is the story behind the taj
is it a symbol of love
a:
Shah Jahan built it as a tomb for **Mumtaz Mahal**, who died on 17 June 1631 giving birth to their **14th child**, a daughter named Gauhar Ara Begum. Court historians say he was devastated: he stayed away from royal affairs for a week and gave up music and fine clothes for two years.

That's why the Taj is remembered as a monument to love. It's also a symbol of Shah Jahan's wealth and power, and its whole plan is meant as **Mumtaz Mahal's mansion in the garden of Paradise**.

q: When was the Taj Mahal built?
alts: how old is the taj mahal
a:
- **1631**: Shah Jahan commissions the tomb after Mumtaz Mahal's death.
- **1632**: construction begins.
- **1643**: the first ceremony at the tomb, the 12th anniversary of her death.
- **1648**: the mausoleum is finished.
- **1653**: the rest of the complex (mosque, jawab, gate, gardens) is completed.

So it's well over 370 years old.

q: How long did it take to build the Taj Mahal?
alts: how many years did it take
a: About **22 years** for the whole complex: construction began in 1632, the mausoleum itself was finished in 1648 (about 16 years), and the surrounding buildings and gardens took another five years, until 1653.

q: How much did the Taj Mahal cost?
alts: what was the cost of building it
a:
The complex cost an estimated **₹32 million** at the time. That's roughly **₹52.8 billion (about US$827 million)** in 2015 money.

It was a heavy burden even for the Mughal Empire at its height; Wikivoyage notes it strained the empire's resources around Agra.

q: How many people worked on the Taj Mahal?
alts: where did the craftsmen come from
a:
More than **20,000** artisans, labourers, painters and others worked on it.

They came from far and wide: sculptors from Bukhara, calligraphers from Syria and Persia, designers from southern India, stone cutters from Baluchistan, and even Italian artisans. Specialists included the Ottoman dome designer Ismail Afandi, the calligrapher Amanat Khan and the finial caster Qazim Khan.

q: Who was the architect of the Taj Mahal?
a:
The chief architect is usually named as **Ustad Ahmad Lahori** (c. 1580–1649), "Master Ahmad of Lahore", Shah Jahan's court architect, from a family of Timurid architects originally from Herat. He's credited with the **Red Fort** in Delhi and may have designed the Taj with Mir Abd-ul Karim and Makramat Khan.

He led a multinational board: the Ottoman dome designer **Ismail Afandi**, Persian architects **Ustad Isa**, **Isa Muhammad Effendi** and **Puru**, the calligrapher **Amanat Khan**, and the finial caster **Qazim Khan**.

q: Who was Mumtaz Mahal?
a:
**Mumtaz Mahal** (born Arjumand Banu Begum, 1593–1631) was Shah Jahan's favourite wife and empress of the Mughal Empire from 1628 until her death. She came from a Persian noble family; her aunt was the powerful empress **Nur Jahan**.

She married Prince Khurram (the future Shah Jahan) in 1612, went with him even on military campaigns, and bore him 14 children. Her title means "the exalted one of the palace".

q: How did Mumtaz Mahal die?
a:
She died on **17 June 1631** in **Burhanpur** in the Deccan, of a haemorrhage after about 30 hours of labour with her 14th child. Shah Jahan was there on a military campaign.

She was first buried in the walled Zainabad garden beside the Tapti river. Her body was later brought to Agra, and a spot in the north-western part of the Taj garden marks where she lay before being moved into the tomb.

q: Who was Shah Jahan?
alts: what else did shah jahan build
a:
**Shah Jahan** (1592–1666), born Prince Khurram, was the fifth Mughal emperor, ruling from 1628 until 1658. His reign is seen as the high point of Mughal architecture: besides the Taj Mahal he built the **Red Fort** and the **Jama Masjid** in Delhi (his new capital, Shahjahanabad) and commissioned the jewelled **Peacock Throne**.

In 1658 his son Aurangzeb deposed him and kept him confined in Agra Fort until he died.

q: What happened to Shah Jahan at the end of his life?
alts: did his son lock him up
could shah jahan see the taj from prison
a:
After Shah Jahan fell ill in 1658, his sons fought over the throne. **Aurangzeb** won, declared his father unfit to rule and confined him in **Agra Fort** from 1658 until his death on 22 January 1666. His daughter **Jahanara** chose to share his confinement and nursed him.

Agra Fort is a short way up the Yamuna, and from it you can see the Taj across the river bend, so the story goes that he spent his last years gazing at his wife's tomb.

q: Who is buried in the Taj Mahal?
alts: is shah jahan buried in the taj mahal
is the emperor buried here too
how many people are buried in the taj
a:
Two people: **Mumtaz Mahal**, at the exact centre of the tomb, and **Shah Jahan**, buried beside her after he died in 1666. Their son Aurangzeb chose to bury him there rather than build him a tomb of his own.

The marble cenotaphs you see in the chamber are memorials; the real graves are in a crypt directly below. Shah Jahan's sits off to the west of hers: the only asymmetrical thing in the whole complex.

q: How many children did Shah Jahan and Mumtaz Mahal have?
alts: how many kids did mumtaz have
a: They had **14 children**, of whom seven survived to adulthood. They included Crown Prince **Dara Shikoh**, Princess **Jahanara Begum** (who later cared for her father in captivity) and **Aurangzeb**, who became the sixth Mughal emperor. Mumtaz died giving birth to the 14th, **Gauhar Ara Begum**.

q: What does Taj Mahal mean?
alts: meaning of the name taj mahal
why is it called the taj mahal
where does the name come from
a: The name is Urdu, drawn from Persian and Arabic: **tāj** means "crown" and **mahal** means "palace", so roughly **"Crown of the Palace"**. Many people also hear in it an echo of **Mumtaz Mahal**, the empress buried there.

q: Where is the Taj Mahal?
alts: what country is the taj in
a:
In **Agra**, in the state of **Uttar Pradesh** in northern India, on the south bank of the **Yamuna** river. Agra is about **200 km** from Delhi; fast trains like the Vande Bharat and Shatabdi expresses do the trip in around two hours.

Agra was a Mughal capital, and **Agra Fort**, also a UNESCO site, is about a 30-minute walk upriver.

q: How tall is the Taj Mahal?
alts: what is the height of the taj mahal
a:
- The whole tomb rises about **73 m (240 ft)** to the tip of its finial.
- The main **dome** is about 23 m tall and sits on a **12 m drum**, topped by a **9.6 m gilded finial**.
- Each of the four **minarets** is more than **40 m (130 ft)** tall.
- The great arches (pishtaqs) on each face are **33 m** high.

q: How big is the Taj Mahal complex?
a:
- The whole complex covers about **17 hectares (42 acres)** and sits on a platform about **300 m** long.
- The tomb stands on a square marble **plinth** about **95.5 m** on each side and 6 m high.
- The tomb itself is a cube with chamfered (cut-off) corners, about **57 m** on each of its long sides.
- The **charbagh** garden is about **300 m** square.

q: What architectural style is the Taj Mahal?
alts: what style of architecture is it
a:
It's the masterpiece of **Mughal architecture**, which blends Persian, Central Asian, Islamic and Indian traditions. The domed tomb in a four-part garden follows earlier Mughal tombs, especially **Humayun's Tomb** in Delhi, and the jewel-like **Tomb of I'timād-ud-Daulah** in Agra, often called the "Baby Taj".

Indian touches include the domed kiosks (**chhatris**) on the roof and the lotus motifs.

q: Is the Taj Mahal perfectly symmetrical?
a:
Almost perfectly. The tomb has four identical faces, the mosque on the west is mirrored by the **jawab** on the east, and the garden is laid out symmetrically along the north–south axis.

The one exception is inside: **Shah Jahan's cenotaph** was added beside Mumtaz Mahal's after his death, so it sits off-centre, to the west of hers.

q: What is the Taj Mahal made of?
alts: where did the marble come from
what stone is it made of
a:
The tomb is built mainly of **brick and lime mortar**, faced inside and out with **white marble** from **Makrana** in Rajasthan. The other buildings use **red sandstone** quarried near **Fatehpur Sikri**.

The white marble is inlaid with **28 kinds of precious and semi-precious stones**, and the calligraphy is in black marble or jasper.

q: How did they move the marble to Agra?
alts: how did they carry the stones
were elephants used to build it
a:
A **15 km** earthen ramp was built to the site, and the marble and other materials were hauled up it on specially built wagons by teams of **oxen and elephants**.

Instead of wooden scaffolding, the builders raised an enormous **brick scaffold** that mirrored the tomb as it grew.

q: What precious stones are in the Taj Mahal?
alts: where did the stones come from
a:
**28 kinds** of precious and semi-precious stones were set into the marble, brought from across Asia:
- **jade** and **crystal** from China
- **turquoise** from Tibet
- **lapis lazuli** from Afghanistan
- **sapphire** from Sri Lanka
- **carnelian** from Arabia
plus jasper, agate, onyx and others. Look closely at the arches here: those red and green flowers are photos of the real inlay.

q: What is pietra dura?
alts: what are the flowers on the walls
a:
**Pietra dura** (Italian for "hard stone"; in India, **parchin kari**) is inlay: thin slices of coloured stone are cut and polished to fit exactly into shapes carved out of the marble, making flowers and vines that look painted but are solid stone.

On the Taj, some single flowers are made from dozens of pieces. Agra's craftsmen still make inlay work today.

q: What does the writing on the Taj Mahal say?
a:
The black lettering framing the arches is **Quranic verse**, written in an ornate **thuluth** script and inlaid in jasper or black marble. The southern gate's inscription roughly translates as: "O Soul, thou art at rest. Return to the Lord at peace with Him, and He at peace with you."

The calligrapher was **Abdul Haq**, whom Shah Jahan honoured with the title **Amanat Khan**. Your guide is named after him, and at the base of the inner dome he signed his work: "Written by the insignificant being, Amanat Khan Shirazi."

q: Why does the calligraphy get bigger toward the top?
alts: are the letters the same size
why are the letters bigger higher up
a: It's an optical correction. Letters higher up the arch are farther from your eye, so the calligraphers made them progressively **larger** toward the top. From the ground, the whole inscription seems to be one even size.

q: What are the carved flowers on the lower walls?
a: Around the base of the walls are **dado** panels with flowers carved in low relief straight into the marble: tulips, irises, lilies and other plants, framed by bands of inlay. Flowers everywhere fit the idea of the tomb as a house in paradise.

q: What is a jali?
alts: what are the windows made of
a:
A **jali** is a screen of stone carved right through into a lattice. The Taj's jalis let in soft light and air while keeping privacy.

The most famous is the **octagonal screen** of eight pierced marble panels around the cenotaphs, inlaid with stones. It replaced an earlier screen of **gold** in 1643.

q: Tell me about the dome.
a:
The main dome is an **onion dome** about **23 m** high, sitting on a **12 m** cylindrical drum (inner diameter 18.4 m), which makes it look even taller. Between drum and dome runs a moulding carved like a **twisted rope**, and the top is decorated with a **lotus** design. It's even slightly asymmetrical.

It's a **double dome**: the ceiling you see inside the tomb is a much lower "false" inner dome, about 25 m above the floor, decorated with a sun motif.

q: What is on top of the dome?
alts: is the top made of gold
a:
A **9.6 m gilded finial** crowns the dome, mixing Persian and Indian design elements and topped by a **crescent moon** whose horns point heavenward, a typical Islamic motif.

It was originally made of **gold**. A Mughal historian recorded that the gold covering was carried off when the Jats raided Agra in the 18th century, and in the early 19th century the finial was replaced by the **gilded bronze** copy you see today.

q: Why do the minarets lean outward?
alts: what are the four towers for
how tall are the four towers
a:
The four **minarets**, each over **40 m** tall, stand at the corners of the plinth. They were built tilted very slightly **outward**, so that if one ever fell, for instance in an earthquake, it would fall away from the tomb instead of onto it.

Each is divided into three almost equal parts by balconies and topped by a chhatri. They echo mosque minarets, where the call to prayer is given, but here they mostly frame the tomb.

q: What are the small domes on the roof?
a: They're **chhatris**, open domed kiosks on columns, a feature of Indian (especially Rajput) architecture. Four sit around the main dome, each minaret is topped by one, and the Great Gate has a row of 22 small ones along its top.

q: What are the big arches on each side?
a: Each face of the tomb has a huge **iwan**, a deep vaulted arch, set in a tall rectangular frame called a **pishtaq**, about 33 m high. On either side are two smaller arched alcoves stacked one above the other, and the same pattern repeats on the cut-off corners.

q: What is the garden called?
alts: why is the garden divided into four
a:
It's a **charbagh**, a Persian-style "four garden". Two main walkways (khiyaban) with water channels divide it into four quarters, and raised paths split each quarter into four **sunken flower beds**, 16 in all, with a walkway round the edge. The design stands for the **gardens of Paradise** and their four rivers.

The first Mughal emperor, **Babur**, brought the charbagh to India. Unusually, the tomb stands at the far end by the river, not in the centre.

q: Did the garden always look like this?
a: No. Originally it was planted with fruit trees and abundant flowers. As the Mughal Empire declined the garden was neglected, and under British rule it was relandscaped with **English-style lawns**. Viceroy **Lord Curzon**'s restoration, finished in 1908, gave it much of the look it still has. Felice Beato's 1858 photo on the board in the garden shows how thickly planted it used to be.

q: What is the raised pool in the middle of the garden?
alts: the pool where the taj reflects
where can i see the reflection
a: At the crossing of the channels is a raised marble tank called **al Hawd al-Kawthar**, the "Tank of Abundance", named after the pool promised to the Prophet Muhammad in paradise. Its still water and the long north–south channel are where the famous **reflection** of the Taj appears. Walk to the edge of the channel here and look down.

q: Is this where Princess Diana sat?
a: Yes: the marble bench on the south side of the raised pool, facing the tomb, is often called the **"Diana bench"** after Princess Diana was photographed sitting there alone in **1992**. It's one of the most popular photo spots in the garden; you'll find it on the pool platform here.

q: How do the fountains work?
alts: how did the fountains get water
a:
Water came from the **Yamuna**. A channel fed an underground reservoir; animal-turned wheels and pulleys lifted it to a tank, and an **aqueduct** carried it round to the garden, where **earthenware pipes** under the ground spread it out.

The central tank's five fountains used large interconnected **copper vessels**, and the drop from walls **9.47 m** high gave the water its pressure.

q: Tell me about the Great Gate.
alts: why does the gate have 22 domes
a:
The **Great Gate** (Darwaza-i-Rauza) is the monumental entrance from the forecourt into the garden. It mirrors the tomb's design in red sandstone, with white marble, bas-relief and pietra dura inlay, and its arch is framed by Quranic calligraphy that roughly translates as **"O Soul, thou art at rest. Return to the Lord at peace with Him, and He at peace with you."**

The row of **22 small domes** on top is popularly said to stand for the 22 years the complex took to build. The gate in this world is textured with a real straight-on photo of it.

q: What is the red building on the west side?
alts: is there a mosque at the taj
why is the taj closed on friday
a: That's the **mosque**, built of red sandstone with three white marble domes, in the same style as other mosques of its time. It faces west, toward Mecca, and it's still used: Friday prayers are held there, which is why the Taj Mahal is **closed to sightseers every Friday**. Its twin on the east side, the jawab, copies it but has no mihrab (prayer niche).

q: What is the building on the east side?
alts: why is there a copy of the mosque
a: That's the **jawab**, Persian for "answer". It copies the mosque exactly to keep the complex symmetrical, but because it faces east, away from Mecca, it can't be used as a mosque. It probably served as a guest house or assembly hall.

q: What is inside the Taj Mahal?
alts: what is in the main chamber
a:
The heart of the tomb is an **octagonal chamber** with 7.3 m sides, its walls about 25 m high up to a false inner dome decorated with a sun motif. In the middle, inside an octagonal marble **jali** screen, are the **cenotaphs** of Mumtaz Mahal and Shah Jahan. A large lamp hangs above them.

Walk through the great south arch and down the corridor here to see it.

q: Are the bodies really in those tombs?
alts: where are mumtaz and shah jahan really buried
a:
No. The two marble boxes in the chamber are **cenotaphs**, false tombs for show, because Muslim tradition discourages elaborate decoration of graves. The **real graves** are in a plainer crypt directly below.

Both lie north–south with the heads to the north, and the bodies were laid on their sides facing west, toward Mecca.

q: What is written on the cenotaphs?
a:
Mumtaz Mahal's cenotaph is inlaid with flowers and Quranic verses, and its epitaph reads: "The illumined grave of Arjumand Bano Begam, entitled Mumtaz Mahal, who died in the year 1631." Shah Jahan's carries his titles and date of death in 1666.

By custom, his has a **pen box** on top (a man's tomb) and hers a flat **writing tablet** (a woman's).

q: What is the lamp hanging inside?
a: The large lamp over the cenotaphs was commissioned by **Lord Curzon**, Viceroy of India, as part of the restoration completed in **1908**. Earlier chandeliers of agate and silver had been carried off in the 18th century by the Jat rulers of Bharatpur.

q: Was there going to be a Black Taj Mahal?
alts: did shah jahan plan a black taj
black marble taj across the river
a:
Probably not. The legend comes from the "fanciful writings" of **Jean-Baptiste Tavernier**, a French traveller and gem merchant who visited Agra in 1665: Shah Jahan supposedly planned a twin tomb in **black marble** across the river, but was deposed before it could be built.

Blackened marble found across the river at **Mehtab Bagh** turned out, after excavation in the 1990s, to be white stone that had darkened. In 2006, archaeologists who rebuilt part of Mehtab Bagh's pool found a likelier origin: the white tomb casts a **dark reflection** in it.

q: Did Shah Jahan cut off the workers' hands?
alts: were the workers hands cut off
is it true the hands were chopped
a: There's **no evidence** for it. Stories that Shah Jahan killed, blinded or cut off the hands of the architects and craftsmen so they could never build anything as beautiful again are myths; historians find nothing to support them. Many of the same craftsmen and their families went on working on other Mughal buildings.

q: Was the Taj Mahal originally a temple?
alts: was it built by someone else
a: No. Claims that someone other than Shah Jahan's builders made it are **not supported by the archaeological record**. In **2000** India's Supreme Court dismissed P. N. Oak's petition claiming a Hindu king built it, and in **2005** the Allahabad High Court dismissed a similar one. In **2015** the Union Minister of Culture told Parliament there was no evidence it was ever a temple, and in **2017** the Archaeological Survey of India said the same.

q: Are there other legends about the Taj Mahal?
Does the Taj Mahal change colour?
a:
It seems to. The polished white marble picks up the light and moisture in the air: it looks **pinkish in the morning**, **milky white** in daylight, **golden** in moonlight, and sometimes even bluish. The sky is part of the design twice over, reflected in the pools and on the building itself.

Try the **Sunrise**, **Day**, **Sunset** and **Moonlight** buttons at the top right (or press **T**) to see it change here.

q: When is the Taj Mahal open?
a:
It's open **every day except Friday**, from **one hour before sunrise to 45 minutes before sunset**. On Fridays it closes to sightseers for prayers at the mosque.

There's also limited **night viewing** around the full moon (except during Ramadan). Times can change, so check the official Archaeological Survey of India site before you go.

q: Can you visit the Taj Mahal at night?
a: Only on special nights: the complex opens for **limited night viewing on the day of the full moon**, except during the month of Ramadan, with small groups booked in advance. Press **Moonlight** at the top right to see it by moonlight here.

q: How much are tickets to the Taj Mahal?
alts: how much does it cost to visit
how much is the entry fee for foreigners
a:
There are three prices, much lower for Indian citizens. As of 2024:
- **₹50** for Indian citizens
- **₹540** for citizens of SAARC and BIMSTEC countries
- **₹1,100** for other foreign visitors
Tickets are sold by the **Archaeological Survey of India** (ASI), online and at the gates. Prices change, so check the official site before you go. Since 2019, visitors who stay more than **three hours** can be fined.

q: What is the best time to visit the Taj Mahal?
alts: best time of day to visit
a:
- **Season:** October to March, when Agra is cool and dry; summers are very hot and the monsoon is humid.
- **Time of day:** go at **opening, around sunrise**, for the softest pink light and the thinnest crowds; late afternoon gives golden light.
- **Avoid Fridays** (closed) and public holidays, when it's packed.

q: How do I get to the Taj Mahal?
alts: how to reach the taj mahal
a:
Agra is about **200 km** from Delhi: fast trains such as the Vande Bharat, Shatabdi or Taj Express take about two to three hours. In Agra, the **Agra Metro** runs between Agra Fort and the Taj, and e-rickshaws and electric buses are easy.

Polluting vehicles aren't allowed near the complex, so you walk or take an electric bus from the parking areas to one of the **three gates**.

q: Can you take photos at the Taj Mahal?
a: Yes in the gardens and grounds, which is where the classic shots are, but **not inside the main tomb chamber**. Expect a security check at the entrance; food and large bags aren't allowed in.

q: How many people visit the Taj Mahal?
alts: how many visitors come each year
how many people visit every year
a: About **five million** people visited in the 2022–23 financial year, making it India's most famous monument and one of the most visited sites in the world. To reduce crowding, visitors who stay longer than three hours can be fined (since 2019).

q: Why is the Taj Mahal turning yellow?
a:
Since the late 20th century **air pollution** has stained the marble yellow-brown; acid rain, industry such as the **Mathura oil refinery** and a polluted Yamuna have all played a part.

In the 1990s, after the Supreme Court case **M. C. Mehta v. Union of India**, India created the **Taj Trapezium Zone**: about 10,400 km² around the monument with strict emission rules. Polluting vehicles are banned near the Taj, and the marble is treated with **mud packs** to bring back its white colour.

q: Was the Taj Mahal ever hidden during a war?
a: Yes. In **1942** the government covered it with scaffolding to disguise it from possible Japanese air attacks, and scaffolding went up again during the India–Pakistan wars of **1965 and 1971** to mislead bomber pilots.

q: Has the Taj Mahal been damaged or looted?
alts: what was stolen from the taj
a: Yes. In the 18th century the **Jat** rulers of Bharatpur raided Agra and carried off two chandeliers (one of agate, one of silver) and, it's said, the gold covering of the finial. By the late 1800s parts of the complex were in poor repair, and Viceroy **Lord Curzon** ordered a major restoration, completed in **1908**. More recently there have been concerns about falling groundwater, cracks and slight tilting of the minarets.

q: Is the Taj Mahal a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
alts: when did it become a world heritage site
is it a world heritage site
a: Yes, since **1983**, cited as "the jewel of Muslim art in India and one of the universally admired masterpieces of the world's heritage". Agra Fort nearby is a World Heritage Site too.

q: Is the Taj Mahal one of the Seven Wonders of the World?
alts: is it a wonder of the world
why isnt it an ancient wonder
a: Yes: in **2007** it was named one of the **New 7 Wonders of the World** in a worldwide poll. It isn't one of the *ancient* Seven Wonders, which were all built more than 2,000 years earlier; you can visit those, including the **Mausoleum at Halicarnassus**, the tomb that gave every mausoleum its name, through **Metaverse Square**: any of the portals here takes you there.

q: What is across the river?
alts: what is on the other side of the yamuna
a:
Across the Yamuna is **Mehtab Bagh**, the "Moonlight Garden", a square charbagh about 300 m on each side, perfectly **aligned with the Taj**. A large octagonal pond on its south edge reflects the tomb.

It had silted up almost completely by the 1990s; excavation and restoration revealed pools, fountains and pavilions, but no foundations of a "Black Taj".

q: Why was the Taj Mahal built next to the river?
a:
Agra's nobles built their tombs and pleasure gardens along the **Yamuna**, which made a grand waterfront city. Placing the tomb at the river end of the garden, instead of in its centre, let it be seen against the open sky and from the river and Agra Fort.

The riverfront terrace was built up on brick foundations, and the river is part of the design: the view north from the terrace looks straight across to Mehtab Bagh.

q: What is Agra Fort?
alts: can you see the taj from agra fort
a: **Agra Fort** is the great red sandstone fortress-palace of the Mughals, about 2.5 km up the Yamuna from the Taj. Akbar rebuilt it and Shah Jahan added white marble palaces; it's where Aurangzeb confined Shah Jahan in his last years. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site too, and the Taj is visible from its riverside terraces.

q: What is the Baby Taj?
a: The **Tomb of I'timād-ud-Daulah** in Agra, built for Mumtaz Mahal's grandfather in the 1620s, is nicknamed the **"Baby Taj"**. It was one of the first Mughal buildings faced in white marble with pietra dura inlay, a clear forerunner of the Taj. **Humayun's Tomb** in Delhi pioneered the big domed tomb in a charbagh garden.

q: Are there copies of the Taj Mahal?
a: The best-known is **Bibi Ka Maqbara** in Aurangabad, built in the 1660s by Aurangzeb's son for his mother and nicknamed the **"Taj of the Deccan"**. Smaller replicas exist around the world, from Bangladesh to casinos in the US.

q: Why is the Taj Mahal so famous?
alts: why do people love the taj
a: Because it combines a moving story, a grieving emperor's monument to his wife, with near-perfect proportions, symmetry and craftsmanship: white marble that changes colour with the light, 28 kinds of inlaid stone, and calligraphy designed to read evenly from the ground. It has become a symbol of India itself. Rabindranath Tagore called it "a teardrop on the cheek of time".

q: What did Tagore say about the Taj Mahal?
alts: teardrop on the cheek of time
a: The poet **Rabindranath Tagore** described the Taj Mahal as **"a teardrop on the cheek of time"**, one of the most quoted lines about it.

q: Is the Taj Mahal solid marble?
alts: what is the platform made of
a:
No. The structure is mostly **brick and lime mortar**, faced with a veneer of white marble outside and in the main chamber. The other buildings and inner surfaces are lined with red sandstone.

Under the tomb, piles were dug and filled with **lime and stone** to form its footings, and the platform above the ground was built of brick and mortar.

q: Which way does the Taj Mahal face?
alts: is the taj facing north or south
where is the main entrance of the tomb
what direction does the taj face
a:
The complex runs exactly **north–south**: you enter from the **south** through the Great Gate, walk north through the garden, and the tomb stands at the **north** end on the Yamuna. All four faces of the tomb are identical, but its main door faces the garden.

The corners are placed so that, seen from the centre, the sun rises and sets over them at the summer and winter solstices, making the Taj a kind of symbolic horizon.

q: What is the town next to the Taj Mahal?
a: South of the complex is **Taj Ganj** (originally called **Mumtazabad**), built with caravanserais, bazaars and markets to serve the workers and visitors. It's still a busy neighbourhood of hotels, cafés and shops.

q: What is the forecourt?
a: Between the town and the Great Gate is the **jilaukhana**, a forecourt where visitors used to dismount and gather before entering. In this world three of the six portals to Metaverse Square stand there.

q: Who was Aurangzeb?
a: **Aurangzeb** (ruled 1658–1707) was Shah Jahan and Mumtaz Mahal's son. He won the war of succession against his brothers, including the crown prince Dara Shikoh, and confined his father in Agra Fort. After Shah Jahan died, Aurangzeb had him buried in the Taj next to Mumtaz.

q: Who was Jahanara Begum?
a: **Jahanara Begum** was the eldest surviving daughter of Shah Jahan and Mumtaz Mahal and one of the most powerful women of the Mughal court. When Aurangzeb confined their father in Agra Fort, she chose to share his eight years of captivity and nursed him until his death. She was also a writer and devoted Sufi, best known for a biography of the Sufi saint **Mu'in ad-Din Chishti**, whom she considered her spiritual master.

q: Who was Nur Jahan?
a: **Nur Jahan** was the chief wife of Emperor Jahangir (Shah Jahan's father) and the real power behind his throne. She was **Mumtaz Mahal's aunt**: Mumtaz's father, Asaf Khan, was her brother. She later backed a rival for the throne and was put under house arrest when Shah Jahan became emperor.

q: Who were the Mughals?
a: The **Mughals** ruled much of the Indian subcontinent from **1526**, when **Babur** founded the empire, into the 18th century. Their great emperors were Babur, Humayun, **Akbar**, **Jahangir**, **Shah Jahan** and **Aurangzeb**. They were famous patrons of architecture, painting and gardens, and the Taj Mahal is the high point of their building.

q: Is the Taj Mahal a religious building?
alts: can you pray at the taj
a: It's a **tomb**, an Islamic mausoleum covered in Quranic verse, not a place of worship itself. The **mosque** on its west side is a working mosque used for Friday prayers, which is why the complex is closed to tourists on Fridays.

q: How much time do I need at the Taj Mahal?
alts: time needed to see the taj
a: Two to three hours is plenty to walk the garden, see the tomb inside and visit the mosque and jawab. Note that since 2019 visitors who stay longer than **three hours** can be fined. Many people combine it with **Agra Fort** (a 30-minute walk) in a day trip from Delhi.

q: What else can I see in Agra?
a:
- **Agra Fort**, the Mughal fortress-palace (UNESCO).
- **Tomb of I'timād-ud-Daulah**, the "Baby Taj".
- **Mehtab Bagh**, the garden across the river with the best sunset view of the Taj.
- **Akbar's Tomb** at Sikandra.
- **Fatehpur Sikri**, Akbar's abandoned red sandstone capital, about 40 km away (UNESCO).
Agra's shops still sell marble inlay work like the Taj's.

Everything here was **built in Blender** from code (blender/build_taj.py), with dimensions taken from Wikipedia's figures, a public-domain site plan and measurements of a straight-on photograph.

The photo boards in the garden credit each photographer. Sizes are close to the real ones, but details are simplified.

q: Why are the other buildings red and the tomb white?
alts: why white marble for the tomb
a:
Red sandstone was the everyday Mughal building stone; white marble was precious. Here only the tomb is white.

The art historian **Ebba Koch** reads the whole plan as two halves: the white tomb and garden stand for the afterlife and paradise, the red sandstone side (forecourt and bazaars) for the worldly side, and the **Great Gate** marks the passage between the two. The white represents Mumtaz Mahal's enlightenment, spirituality and faith.

q: Could the Taj Mahal survive an earthquake?
a: It has stood for more than 370 years, and the minarets were deliberately tilted outward so they would fall away from the tomb in a collapse. There are modern worries, though: falling groundwater in the Yamuna basin, cracks noted in parts of the tomb in 2010, and signs of slight tilting in the minarets. The Archaeological Survey of India monitors it closely.

q: When was Mumtaz Mahal born?
alts: how old was mumtaz when she died
a: She was born **Arjumand Banu Begum** on **27 April 1593** in **Agra**, into a Persian noble family. Her father was **Asaf Khan**, a powerful Mughal official, and her aunt was the empress **Nur Jahan**. She died in 1631, aged 38.

q: When did Shah Jahan marry Mumtaz Mahal?
alts: how did shah jahan meet mumtaz
wedding of shah jahan and mumtaz
a: They were betrothed in **1607** and married five years later, in **1612**, in Agra, when she was 19 and he was 20 (still Prince Khurram). After the wedding he gave her the title **Mumtaz Mahal**. They were married for 19 years and had 14 children.

q: What does the name Mumtaz Mahal mean?
a: **Mumtaz Mahal** means roughly "the exalted one of the palace"; her birth name was Arjumand Banu Begum. When Shah Jahan became emperor in 1628 he made her chief empress with titles including **Padshah Begum** ("first lady") and **Malika-i-Jahan** ("Queen of the World").

q: What was Mumtaz Mahal like?
alts: what kind of person was mumtaz
did mumtaz travel with shah jahan
a: Court writers describe her as Shah Jahan's constant companion; she even travelled with him on military campaigns, which is how she came to die far from home in Burhanpur. Unlike her aunt Nur Jahan she showed **no ambition for political power**. She lived with Shah Jahan in the richly decorated **Khas Mahal** in Agra Fort and looked after a riverside garden in Agra now called **Zahara Bagh**.

q: How many wives did Shah Jahan have?
alts: did shah jahan have other wives
a: Several. He married **Kandahari Begum** in 1610, **Mumtaz Mahal** in 1612 and **Izz-un-Nissa (Akbarabadi Mahal)** in 1617, among others. Mumtaz was by far his favourite. His other wives are buried in mausoleums **outside the Taj complex walls**.

q: When was Shah Jahan born?
alts: how old was shah jahan when he died
a: He was born **Prince Khurram** on **5 January 1592** in **Lahore** (in today's Pakistan), the third son of Prince Salim, later Emperor **Jahangir**. His grandfather **Akbar** doted on him and had him raised in his own household. He died in January 1666, aged 74.

q: What does Shah Jahan mean?
alts: meaning of the name shah jahan
why was he called shah jahan
a: **Shah Jahan** is Persian for **"King of the World"**, the regnal name Prince Khurram took when he became emperor in 1628.

q: When did Shah Jahan rule?
alts: how did shah jahan become emperor
a: From **1628 to 1658**. When Jahangir died in 1627, Shah Jahan's father-in-law **Asaf Khan** outmanoeuvred Nur Jahan's favourite, Prince Shahryar, and Shah Jahan was crowned in **Agra Fort**. His reign is called the **golden age of Mughal architecture**. It ended when his son Aurangzeb deposed him in 1658.

q: How did Shah Jahan react to Mumtaz's death?
alts: what did shah jahan do after mumtaz died
how much did he love her
a: Court historians say he was **"paralysed by grief"**. He stayed away from royal affairs for a week, and for **two years** gave up listening to music and wearing lavish clothes. Contemporary writers said he never showed anyone else the affection he had shown her.

q: What else did Shah Jahan build?
alts: did shah jahan build the red fort
a:
A great deal; his reign is the **golden age of Mughal architecture**:
- the **Red Fort** and the **Jama Masjid** in Delhi, centre of his new capital **Shahjahanabad**
- the **Shalimar Gardens** in Lahore, and a renovation of Lahore Fort
- white marble palaces and mosques inside **Agra Fort**
- the jewelled **Peacock Throne**
He preferred elegant refinement to sheer size.

q: What is the Peacock Throne?
a: The **Peacock Throne** (Takht-e-Taus) was the fabulously jewelled throne Shah Jahan had made to celebrate his reign, one of the most famous treasures of the Mughal court.

q: Who was Ustad Ahmad Lahori?
alts: tell me about ustad ahmad lahori
what else did the architect design
a: **Ustad Ahmad Lahori** (c. 1580–1649), also called Ahmad Mi'mar ("Ahmad the Architect"), was Shah Jahan's chief architect, from a family of Timurid architects originally from Herat. He's credited with designing the **Red Fort** in Delhi, helped lay out the new capital Shahjahanabad, and is generally named as the lead designer of the Taj. His style blends Indo-Islamic and Persian architecture.

q: Who was Amanat Khan?
alts: who is the guide named after
a: **Amanat Khan** was the title Shah Jahan gave **Abdul Haq**, the chief calligrapher of the Taj Mahal, who came from Shiraz in Persia. He designed the flowing **thuluth** inscriptions of Quranic verse on the arches and gate, and signed his work at the base of the inner dome: "Written by the insignificant being, Amanat Khan Shirazi." I'm named after him.

q: Who else helped design and build the Taj Mahal?
a:
A multinational board worked under Ustad Ahmad Lahori:
- **Ismail Afandi**, an Ottoman dome designer
- the Persian architects **Ustad Isa**, **Isa Muhammad Effendi** and **Puru**
- **Amanat Khan Shirazi**, chief calligrapher
- **Qazim Khan**, who cast the finial
- masonry supervisors **Muhammad Hanif**, **Mir Abdul Karim** and **Mukkarimat**
The garden may have been designed by **Ali Mardan**, who is linked to the similar Shalimar Gardens.

q: Who was Gauhar Ara Begum?
a: **Gauhar Ara Begum** ("adorned in gems") was the 14th and youngest child of Shah Jahan and Mumtaz Mahal, born on **17 June 1631**, the day her mother died. She survived and lived about 75 years, until around **1706**, keeping a low profile through the reigns of her father and her brother Aurangzeb.

q: Who was Dara Shikoh?
alts: who was the heir to the throne
a: **Dara Shikoh** (1615–1659) was Shah Jahan and Mumtaz Mahal's eldest son and Shah Jahan's chosen heir, named heir-apparent in 1633. When Shah Jahan fell ill in 1658, Dara acted as regent, but his brother **Aurangzeb** defeated him in the war of succession and had him **executed in 1659**. He's buried in Humayun's Tomb in Delhi.

q: Who was Jahangir?
a: **Jahangir** (born Prince Salim) was the fourth Mughal emperor, who ruled from 1605 until his death in 1627. He was Shah Jahan's father and the husband of **Nur Jahan**, Mumtaz Mahal's aunt. Shah Jahan succeeded him after a struggle with his half-brother Shahryar.

q: Who was Akbar?
a: **Akbar** was the third Mughal emperor and Shah Jahan's grandfather. He made **Agra** his capital in 1558, rebuilt **Agra Fort** in red sandstone between 1565 and 1573, and built a whole new city, **Fatehpur Sikri**, nearby. He was so fond of the young Khurram that he raised him in his own household.

q: Who was Babur?
alts: who brought the charbagh to india
a: **Babur**, from Central Asia, founded the Mughal Empire in **1526** after the First Battle of Panipat. He brought the Persian **charbagh** garden to India, the four-part paradise garden that frames the Taj Mahal.

q: Who was Mumtaz Mahal's father?
alts: who was abul hasan asaf khan
a: **Abu'l-Hasan Asaf Khan**, a wealthy noble who held high office in the Mughal Empire and was the brother of the empress **Nur Jahan**. As grand vizier he secured the throne for his son-in-law Shah Jahan in 1627.

q: Who was Mumtaz Mahal's grandfather?
a: **Mirza Ghiyas Beg**, a Persian who entered Akbar's service in Agra in 1577 and rose to be prime minister under Jahangir, with the title **I'timād-ud-Daulah** ("Pillar of the State"). His daughter Nur Jahan built his tomb in Agra, the jewel-like "**Baby Taj**".

q: Who owned the land where the Taj Mahal stands?
alts: how did shah jahan get the land
what was here before the taj
a: The site, on the Yamuna just south of walled Agra, held a mansion belonging to **Raja Jai Singh I**. Shah Jahan loved the spot and chose it for the tomb, and Jai Singh gave it to him in exchange for a **large palace in the centre of Agra**.

q: Who was Jean-Baptiste Tavernier?
alts: french traveller who visited the taj
who started the black taj story
a: **Jean-Baptiste Tavernier** was a French traveller and gem merchant who visited Agra in **1665**. His writings are the source of the legend that Shah Jahan planned a **Black Taj** across the river, a story historians treat as fanciful. Some 19th-century theories that a Frenchman designed the Taj also leaned on his work.

q: Who was Lord Curzon?
a: **Lord Curzon** was the British viceroy of India who, at the end of the 19th century, ordered a major restoration of the Taj Mahal, completed in **1908**. He also commissioned the large **lamp** in the tomb chamber and replaced the overgrown garden with the **European-style lawns** you still see.

q: Who is Ebba Koch?
a: **Ebba Koch** is an art historian and leading expert on Mughal architecture and the Taj Mahal. She reads the whole complex as a picture of earthly life and the afterlife: a white marble half (tomb and garden, the otherworldly side) mirrored by a red sandstone half for the worldly markets, with the Great Gate as the passage between them.

q: Did Nur Jahan support Shah Jahan?
a: No, they became rivals. Nur Jahan backed her son-in-law **Shahryar** for the throne and sent Shah Jahan on distant campaigns; he even rebelled against his father in 1622. After Jahangir's death in 1627 Shah Jahan won the succession and put Nur Jahan under house arrest, where she lived quietly until her death.

q: What was the war of succession?
alts: why did aurangzeb fight his brothers
what happened when shah jahan got sick
a: When Shah Jahan fell ill in **1658**, his sons fought for the throne. **Aurangzeb**, the third son, defeated his brothers, executed the crown prince **Dara Shikoh** and the others, declared his father unfit to rule even after he recovered, and confined him in Agra Fort until his death in 1666.

q: How were the foundations built?
alts: what are the foundations of the taj
how does it stand by the river
a: About **1.2 hectares** was excavated, filled with earth to reduce seepage, and levelled **50 m** above the riverbank. Under the tomb, piles were dug and filled with **lime and stone** to form the footings, and a brick-and-mortar platform was built on top.

q: How did they lift the heavy stones?
alts: how did they get water for building
a: An elaborate **post-and-beam pulley system** raised the blocks into place, and a giant **brick scaffold** that mirrored the tomb gave the builders access. Materials came up a **15 km earthen ramp** on wagons pulled by oxen and elephants, and water was drawn from the river by animal-powered devices.

q: When was the first ceremony at the Taj Mahal?
a: On **6 February 1643**, while the building was only partly finished, Shah Jahan held an observance there for the **12th anniversary** of Mumtaz Mahal's death.

q: Did the Taj Mahal ever leak?
alts: was there damage after it was built
a: Yes, early on. In **December 1652** Prince Aurangzeb wrote to his father that the tomb, the mosque and the assembly hall had developed extensive **leaks** during the previous rainy season.

q: What did the Mughals call the Taj Mahal?
alts: what was it called in shah jahan's time
a: In his 1636 chronicle, the **Padshahnama**, the court historian Abdul Hamid Lahori calls it **rauza-i munawwara**, "the illumined (or illustrious) tomb". The name "Taj Mahal" may also echo the second half of "Mumtaz".

q: Where was Mumtaz Mahal buried before the tomb was ready?
alts: was mumtaz buried in the garden
where did her body go first
how was her body moved to agra
a: First in **Burhanpur**, in the walled Zainabad garden by the Tapti river, where she died. Her body was then brought to Agra; a place in the **north-western quarter** of the Taj garden marks where she lay before being moved to her final resting place inside the tomb.

q: Was there once a gold screen around the tombs?
alts: what was there before the marble screen
a: Yes. For the **second anniversary** of Mumtaz Mahal's death, in 1633, the cenotaphs were surrounded by a screen made of **gold**. It was replaced in **1643** by the octagonal pierced **marble** screen you see today.

q: Who looks after the Taj Mahal?
a: The **Archaeological Survey of India** (ASI), which has maintained it since independence in **1947**. The Taj, its grounds and its buildings are a **Monument of National Importance**. A 2025 government report said it earned **₹297 crore** (about US$31 million) in five years, the most of any ASI monument.

q: Did the British plan to demolish the Taj Mahal?
alts: was the taj going to be sold
did someone try to destroy the taj
a: There's **no evidence** for it. The story that **Lord William Bentinck**, governor-general in the 1830s, planned to demolish the Taj and auction its marble seems to have grown out of his fund-raising sale of discarded marble from **Agra Fort**, according to his biographer.

q: Has the Taj Mahal been damaged recently?
a: Minor damage was reported after storms on **11 April 2018** and **31 May 2020**, and cracks were noted in parts of the tomb in 2010, with signs of slight tilting in the minarets. In the 2020s the government has applied **mud packs** to restore the white colour and replaced broken marble.

q: Was building the Taj Mahal hard on the people?
alts: was it a burden on the empire
a: It was a heavy burden. Even at the height of the empire, building the Taj strained Mughal resources, and Wikivoyage notes it caused a small **famine** around Agra. The complex cost about **₹32 million** at the time.

q: Was the Taj Mahal designed by a European?
alts: did an italian design the taj
a: No. In 1879 Henry George Keene promoted the idea that an Italian, **Geronimo Veroneo**, designed it, and others claimed a Frenchman, **Austin of Bordeaux**. Both theories rest on misread travellers' accounts and have no support; the Taj was designed by Shah Jahan's own board of architects under Ustad Ahmad Lahori.

q: Did the builders promise never to build anything like it again?
alts: contracts not to copy the taj
were craftsmen forbidden to work again
a: Some stories say the craftsmen signed contracts promising never to work on a similar design, and darker ones claim they were mutilated. **No evidence** supports either; historians treat them as legends.

q: What is the plinth?
alts: what is the platform the taj stands on
what is the floor pattern around the plinth
a: The tomb and minarets stand on a square white marble **plinth** about **6 m** high and **95.5 m** on each side. Around it, the main platform is paved with an interlocking pattern of **white marble octagons set into red sandstone four-pointed stars**, framed by a border.

q: What does the whole complex stand on?
alts: how big is the riverfront platform
what is the terrace made of
a: The complex sits on a platform about **300 m** long and **8.7 m** high on the bank of the Yamuna, laid out in patterns of dark and light sandstone. The terrace between the mosque and the jawab, where the tomb stands, overlooks the river.

q: How do you get up onto the plinth?
alts: how do i get onto the marble platform
a: On the south side of the plinth, facing the garden, there are **two flights of stairs**, partly covered, on either side. They are the only way up from ground level to the tomb. In this world they're on the south face of the plinth, either side of the centre.

q: Why does the tomb have cut-off corners?
alts: how many sides does the tomb have
a: The tomb is a large multi-chambered cube with its four corners **chamfered** (cut off), which turns it into an eight-sided building about **57.3 m** across on each long side. The pattern of arches on the main faces repeats in miniature on the cut corners, so the design is symmetrical from every direction.

q: What is the hasht-behesht plan?
a: **Hasht-behesht** (Persian, "eight paradises") is a plan with a central domed hall surrounded by eight rooms, used for pavilions and tombs. The Taj's plan follows it, inspired, like its charbagh garden, by **Humayun's Tomb** in Delhi.

q: What buildings inspired the Taj Mahal?
alts: what was the taj based on
a: It grew out of Timurid and Mughal tombs: the **Gur-e Amir** in Samarkand, tomb of Timur, ancestor of the Mughals, and **Humayun's Tomb** in Delhi, which gave it the charbagh garden and the hasht-behesht plan. The jewel-like **Tomb of I'timād-ud-Daulah** in Agra pioneered the white marble and pietra dura.

q: What is the drum under the dome?
a: The dome sits on a **12 m** high cylindrical **drum** with an inner diameter of **18.4 m**, which lifts it high above the roof. Where drum and dome meet, a moulding is carved like a **twisted rope**.

q: What is the lotus design on the dome?
alts: lotus on top of the dome
flower at the top of the dome
a: The top of the main dome, and of the four small domes, is decorated with a **lotus** design, an Indian motif, from which the gilded finial rises. It's one of the ways the Taj blends Persian and Indian traditions.

q: What are the thin spires on the corners?
alts: small towers on the roof edge
a: They're **guldastas**, tall slender pinnacles rising from the edges of the walls, beside each great arch and at the corners. They're decorative, adding to the building's lightness and vertical lift.

q: What are the four small domed pavilions around the main dome for?
alts: do the small domes have a purpose
a: The four **chhatris** at the corners of the roof repeat the onion shape of the main dome. They stand on columns over the roof and help bring **light** into the building, besides framing the great dome.

q: Are there stairs inside the minarets?
alts: how do you get to the top of the minaret
a: Yes. Steps lead up inside each minaret to the top, where rectangular openings below the little dome let in light and air. Each tower is split into three nearly equal parts by balconies and topped by a chhatri.

q: What are the smaller arches beside the big arch?
a: On either side of each great arch (pishtaq) are **two smaller arched balconies stacked one above the other**. The same pattern repeats, smaller, on the chamfered corners.

q: What do the inside walls look like?
a: Inside, **two tiers of eight arches** line the octagonal chamber, echoing the outside. The four central upper arches are balconies whose outer windows have intricate **jali** screens. The walls are covered in carved flower dados, gemstone inlay and calligraphy panels, up to about **25 m**, where a false inner dome with a **sun motif** closes the room.

q: How does light get inside the tomb?
a: Mostly through **jali screens**: the inner walls are open along the main axes, fitted with pierced marble screens that filter daylight into the chamber, and the upper balconies have jali windows too. The four roof **chhatris** help bring light in, and a lamp hangs over the cenotaphs.

q: Are there other rooms in the tomb?
alts: how many rooms in the taj
a: Yes. On three sides of the main chamber are elongated rooms flanked by small square cells with decorated ceilings, probably used by visitors and **Quran reciters** to rest. Staircases lead from the ground floor up to the roof, with corridors and a system of ventilation shafts.

q: What is in the crypt below the tomb?
a: From the southern entrance room a stairway leads down to the **lower tomb chamber**: a rectangular room with marble walls and a plain coved ceiling, where Mumtaz Mahal and Shah Jahan are actually buried. Mumtaz's real tomb is largely undecorated except for the **Ninety-Nine Names of God** inscribed on its side.

q: How is the screen around the cenotaphs made?
alts: how many panels in the jali
is the screen carved from one piece
a: It's made of **eight marble panels**, each carved right through into fine lattice (mahjar-i mushabbak) and inlaid with semi-precious stones, forming an octagon round the two cenotaphs. It was installed in **1643**, replacing a screen of gold.

q: What does Shah Jahan's cenotaph say?
alts: what is written on shah jahan's tomb
a: Surrounded by inlaid red poppies, it reads: "This is the sacred grave of His Most Exalted Majesty, Dweller in Paradise, Second Lord of the Auspicious Conjunction, Shah Jahan, Padshah; may it ever be fragrant! The year 1076" (AD 1666). His real tomb below carries a longer epitaph giving his death on the 26th of Rajab, 1076 AH.

q: How are the red sandstone buildings decorated?
alts: white lines on the red buildings
a: The domes and vaults of the sandstone buildings carry incised and painted tracery in elaborate geometric forms, and **herringbone** inlays fill the spaces between elements. As a rule, **white** inlay is used on red sandstone and **dark** inlay on white marble, and floors and walkways are laid in contrasting tiles in tessellated patterns.

q: Why are there no people or animals in the decoration?
a: In line with the Islamic avoidance of human and animal figures in religious settings, the decoration keeps to three kinds: **calligraphy**, **abstract** geometric forms and **plant** motifs: flowers, vines and fruit, carved, inlaid in stone or painted.

q: What script is the calligraphy written in?
alts: what is the writing made of
a: Mostly **thuluth**, a flowing, ornate Arabic script, made of **jasper or black marble** inlaid into white marble panels. The higher panels use slightly larger letters to cancel out the foreshortening when you look up at them.

q: Where did pietra dura come from?
a: The technique appeared in **Rome** in the 16th century and matured in **Florence**. By the early 1600s Florentine inlaid objects had reached the Mughal court, where the art was reinterpreted in an Indian style called **parchin kari**. Its most sumptuous expression is the Taj Mahal.

q: Can I buy inlay work like the Taj's in Agra?
a: Yes. Because of the Taj there's a flourishing **pietra dura** industry in Agra, and many shops sell marble boxes, plaques and jewellery with inlay resembling the Taj's. Agra's famous sweet is **petha**.

q: How many flower beds are in the garden?
a: **Sixteen.** Two main walkways (**khiyaban**) divide the garden into four quarters, raised paths split each quarter into four **sunken** beds (parterres), and a walkway runs round the outside connecting them all.

q: How many fountains are in the central tank?
a: The raised marble tank in the centre of the garden has **five fountains**, and more fountains run along the avenues and channels. Its long reflecting pool runs north–south to hold the image of the tomb.

q: What plants grew in the garden originally?
alts: what flowers were in the garden
how did the garden look in mughal times
a: Early accounts describe a garden overflowing with plants: abundant **roses**, **daffodils** and **fruit trees**, with avenues of trees and fountains. It was neglected as the empire declined, and under British rule it was relandscaped as formal lawns.

q: Is the river part of the garden's design?
alts: was the river planned into the garden
mehtab bagh and the taj garden
a: Probably. Since **Mehtab Bagh** was rediscovered on the opposite bank, the Archaeological Survey of India has suggested that the **Yamuna** itself was built into the design, meant to be seen as one of the **rivers of Paradise** flowing between two gardens.

q: Who designed the garden?
a: Possibly **Ali Mardan**. The Taj garden's layout and features are so similar to the **Shalimar Gardens** in Lahore that both may have been designed by him.

q: What does the four-part garden symbolise?
a: The charbagh represents the gardens of **Paradise** described in the Quran's 55th chapter, Ar-Rahman ("And for him who fears to stand before his Lord are two gardens…"), and its four water channels stand for the four rivers of Paradise named in a hadith: Sayhan, Jayhan, the Euphrates and the Nile.

q: Is the Taj Mahal complex walled?
a: Yes, on three sides: **crenellated red sandstone walls** enclose the garden, while the side facing the Yamuna is open. Along the inside of the walls run columned arcades with domed chhatris and smaller buildings such as the **Music House**.

q: Is anyone else buried at the Taj Mahal complex?
alts: tombs of shah jahan's other wives
a: Inside the tomb, only Mumtaz Mahal and Shah Jahan. **Outside the complex walls** there are other mausoleums for Shah Jahan's other wives, royals and favourite servants.

q: How many entrances does the Taj Mahal have?
alts: east gate west gate south gate
a: Visitors come in through **three gates** into the forecourt, then walk through the Great Gate into the garden. Polluting vehicles aren't allowed near the complex, so people walk or take **electric buses** from the parking areas.

q: What does the Great Gate symbolise?
alts: why is the gate in the middle
a: In Ebba Koch's reading, the complex is split into a **worldly** red sandstone half (forecourt and bazaars) and an **otherworldly** half (the garden and white tomb), mirror images of each other. The Great Gate in the middle marks the **passage between the two worlds**, and stepping through it you see Paradise laid out ahead.

q: What is a mihrab?
alts: why does the jawab have no mihrab
direction of mecca in the mosque
a: A **mihrab** is the niche in a mosque's wall that shows the direction of Mecca, which worshippers face to pray. The Taj's mosque has one on its west side; the **jawab**, its mirror image, lacks a mihrab, since it faces the wrong way, and has inlaid patterns on its floor instead.

q: What was the purpose of the jawab?
alts: what was the copy of the mosque for
a: Mainly **symmetry**: it balances the mosque. It probably served as a **guest house** or assembly hall; a 1652 letter from Aurangzeb mentions the complex's "assembly hall" leaking.

q: Where is Makrana?
alts: where does the marble come from exactly
a: **Makrana** is a town in **Rajasthan**, about 110 km west of Jaipur. It supplied the Taj's white marble, and many of its craftsmen and stonemasons. **Makrana marble** has been recognised as a Global Heritage Stone Resource by the International Union of Geological Sciences.

q: Where does the red sandstone come from?
a: The red sandstone was quarried near **Fatehpur Sikri** in Uttar Pradesh, the old Mughal capital of Akbar, about 40 km from Agra.

q: Can I drive up to the Taj Mahal?
alts: how do i get from the parking
a: No. To protect the marble from pollution, polluting vehicles aren't allowed near the complex. You park in the designated areas and **walk** or ride an **electric bus**, tonga (horse cart) or e-rickshaw to one of the three gates.

q: Is there a time limit for visiting?
a: Yes. Since **2019**, to fight overcrowding, visitors who stay longer than **three hours** can be fined.

q: Are there scams or touts at the Taj Mahal?
a: Wikivoyage warns that touts and hawkers swarm Agra's monuments, but **inside the Taj complex** it's free of scams and touts. Buy tickets from the official counters or the ASI website.

q: What food is Agra famous for?
a: Agra's speciality is **petha**, a very sweet translucent candy (try the plain ivory one or the yellow angoori), and **dal moth**, a spicy lentil mix. Spicy **chaat** stalls draw crowds all over town.

q: What is the Taj Mahotsav?
a: The **Taj Mahotsav** ("Taj Festival") is a 10-day event held every year from **18 to 27 February** at Shilpgram in Agra, inspired by Mughal-era culture. About **400 artisans** from all over India show their crafts, from Agra's marble inlay and zardozi embroidery to Kashmiri shawls, alongside music and dance.

q: Do famous people visit the Taj Mahal?
a: Often: foreign dignitaries regularly visit the Taj on trips to India. The best-known photo is of **Princess Diana** sitting alone on the marble bench by the central pool in 1992, which is still called the "Diana bench".

q: How much money does the Taj Mahal make?
a: A 2025 government report said the Taj earned about **₹297 crore** (around US$31 million) over five years, making it the highest-earning monument run by the Archaeological Survey of India.

q: Tell me about Agra.
a: **Agra**, in Uttar Pradesh about 200 km from Delhi, was a Mughal capital: Akbar made it his capital in 1558. It's home to two UNESCO World Heritage Sites, the **Taj Mahal** and **Agra Fort**, with a third, **Fatehpur Sikri**, nearby. Today it's a busy tourist city known for marble inlay work and petha sweets.

q: What is the Taj Trapezium Zone?
a: A protected area of about **10,400 km²** around Agra, shaped like a trapezium, covering three Mughal World Heritage Sites (**Taj Mahal, Agra Fort, Fatehpur Sikri**) and over 40 other monuments. It was set up in the 1990s after the Supreme Court's **M. C. Mehta v. Union of India** ruling: industries there may not burn coke or coal, and the courts limit tree felling, construction and industrial expansion.

q: How is the marble cleaned?
alts: how do they keep it white
a: With **mud packs**: a layer of clay is spread on the stained marble and washed off once dry, drawing out grime and restoring the white colour. In the 2020s the government has used them alongside replacing broken marble.

q: What is Humayun's Tomb?
a: **Humayun's Tomb** in Delhi, built 1565–1572 for the second Mughal emperor and commissioned by his widow **Bega Begum**, was the **first garden-tomb** on the subcontinent, designed by the Persian architects Mirak Mirza Ghiyas and his son. Modelled on Timur's Gur-e Amir, it set the pattern that reached its peak in the Taj. Shah Jahan's son **Dara Shikoh** is buried there.

q: Who built the Baby Taj?
alts: nur jahan tomb for her father
a: The empress **Nur Jahan** built it between **1622 and 1628** for her father, Mirza Ghiyas Beg (I'timād-ud-Daulah), Mumtaz Mahal's grandfather. Often called a "jewel box" and a draft of the Taj, it moved Mughal tombs from red sandstone toward **white marble and pietra dura**. Unlike most Mughal tombs it has no central dome.

q: What is the Taj of the Deccan?
alts: copy of the taj in aurangabad
azam shah tomb for his mother
a: **Bibi Ka Maqbara** in Aurangabad, commissioned in **1660** by Prince **Azam Shah**, Aurangzeb's son, for his mother **Dilras Banu Begum**. It strikingly resembles the Taj Mahal, the tomb of Aurangzeb's own mother, and is nicknamed the "Taj of the Deccan".

q: What is Fatehpur Sikri?
a: **Fatehpur Sikri** is the red sandstone city the emperor **Akbar** built near Agra in the 16th century and later abandoned. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and its quarries supplied the red sandstone for the Taj complex.

q: How far is Agra Fort from the Taj Mahal?
a: About **2.5 km** northwest, up the Yamuna, about a 30-minute walk. Akbar rebuilt the fort in red sandstone (1565–1573) and Shah Jahan added white marble palaces after 1628, including the Musamman Burj. It's where Aurangzeb confined Shah Jahan, who could see the Taj from there.

q: What are the New 7 Wonders of the World?
alts: when were the new wonders chosen
how was the taj chosen as a wonder
what are the new seven wonders
a: Chosen in a worldwide online and telephone poll announced on **7 July 2007** in Lisbon: the **Taj Mahal**, the **Great Wall of China**, **Petra**, **Christ the Redeemer**, **Machu Picchu**, **Chichén Itzá** and the **Colosseum**, with the Great Pyramid of Giza as an honorary candidate. The poll was criticised as unscientific because people could vote more than once.

q: What is the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus?
alts: why is there a portal to the mausoleum
where does the word mausoleum come from
a: The tomb of **Mausolus**, a ruler in what is now Turkey, built in the 4th century BCE and one of the ancient **Seven Wonders**. It was so famous that every grand tomb since has been called a **mausoleum**, including the Taj. You can reach it from **Metaverse Square**, which any portal here takes you to.

q: Is the Taj Mahal only a symbol of love?
a: No. Besides love it's a symbol of Shah Jahan's **wealth and power** and of a prospering empire. Its strict symmetry about a central axis expresses a ruler who brings **balance and harmony**, and its whole plan is meant as **Mumtaz Mahal's mansion in the garden of Paradise**. Today it's a symbol of India itself.

q: Why does the Taj reflect the sky?
alts: presence of god in the design
a: The sky is built into the design twice: in the reflecting pools and on the polished marble itself, which takes on the colours of the sky through the day. Some see this as a way of implying the presence of God at the site.

q: What can I do here?
alts: things to do in this world
a:
A good walk:
- through the **Great Gate** from the forecourt for the classic first view
- down the garden to the **lotus pool** and Diana's bench, and look into the channel for the reflection
- up the **stairs** onto the plinth and through the great south arch
- down the corridor into the **tomb chamber** to see the cenotaphs and the jali screen
- out to the **riverfront terrace**, then the **mosque** and **jawab**
Read the photo boards on the way, and try the time-of-day buttons. The map in the corner (M) shows where you are and the exits. I can also take you to any of these: use the buttons in this chat.

q: What are the photo boards?
a: They're **real photographs** of the Taj Mahal from Wikimedia Commons, from Felice Beato's 1858 view to close-ups of the calligraphy and inlay, each credited to its photographer and licence. Several of them are the very photos this world's textures were made from.

q: How accurate is this model?
alts: what is different from the real taj
a: The main dimensions follow the real ones: the 95.5 m plinth, the 57.3 m tomb, the dome on its drum, minarets over 40 m, and a 300 m square garden, measured from Wikipedia's figures, a public-domain site plan and a straight-on photo. Details are simplified: the garden's planting, the inner rooms and crypt, and much of the carving and inlay are approximations, and the surroundings beyond the walls are invented.

q: Who made this world?
a: It was made by **Ayush Rajpal**, as a world on the **Metaverse Web**, a network of linked 3D worlds you walk between through portals. The model was built in Blender from code, the textures from real photographs, and I, the guide, am a Labubu like the guides in the Metaverse Web's Seven Wonders worlds.

q: Why is the guide a Labubu?
alts: why do you look like that
a: The guides in the Metaverse Web's Seven Wonders worlds are all **Labubus** dressed for their place and period, so I'm dressed as a Mughal calligrapher: a white jama robe, a gold sash, a turban with a jewel and plume, and a reed pen.

There are six portals, all leading to **Metaverse Square**, in three places marked **EXIT** on the map (press **M**):
